dropped.reason: Asks for a labelled diagram of Huygens' wave model, which cannot be answered or marked as text.
Requires measuring the printed figure with a ruler, which is marked 'not to scale', so it can't be answered reliably as text.

questions.question: Which statement about an object undergoing projectile motion is correct? (Point $Y$ is the highest point of the path.)
questions.answer: Launch and impact are at the same height (ground), so the potential energy is the same and, with no air resistance, the kinetic energy is the same (C). At $Y$ the vertical velocity is zero but the horizontal velocity is not, so $E_K\ne0$, and the potential energy at $Y$ is a maximum. Also $E_K$ at launch equals $E_K$ at $Y$ plus $E_P$ at $Y$, not $E_P$ alone.
options: Its kinetic energy at point $Y$ will be zero.
Its potential energy at point $Y$ is a minimum.
Its kinetic energy will be the same at launch as it is at impact.
Its kinetic energy on launch will be the same as the potential energy at point $Y$.

questions.question: Which is a correct expression for the total energy of an orbiting satellite? ($U$ is the gravitational potential energy and $E_K$ the kinetic energy.)
questions.answer: $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}$ and $E_K=\frac12mv^2=\frac{GMm}{2r}$, so $E_K=-\frac U2$ and $E_{total}=E_K+U=-E_K=\frac U2$ (C).

questions.question: Two satellites are in the same Low Earth Orbit. Satellite $X$ has four times the mass of satellite $Y$. What is the ratio of their orbital speeds?
questions.answer: $\frac{mv^2}{r}=\frac{GMm}{r^2}$ gives $v=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$, which is independent of the satellite's mass. Same orbit means the same speed, a ratio of $1:1$ (A).

questions.question: Students discuss the best way to increase speed when on a swing in a children's playground. Which statement is correct and supported by physics principles?
questions.answer: Raising the centre of mass at the top of the swing does work, adding gravitational potential energy to the system, which becomes extra kinetic energy as the swing descends. (B is the school's answer. The rope force acts through the pivot, so it provides no torque about it, ruling out C.)
options: Straighten your legs at top of swing to increase speed, as the leg movement adds to available kinetic energy.
At top of swing, straighten your legs and pull on the support ropes, because both actions raise your centre of mass, adding potential energy.
Pull on the support ropes at top of swing to provide a torque around the pivot point where the rope is attached.
At top of swing, straighten your legs and pull on the support ropes, because both use force and therefore increase the centripetal acceleration.

questions.question: The diagram shows an electron which moves with a constant velocity, entering an electric field at a right angle. Which alternative describes the path of the electron in the electric field?
questions.answer: The field points down the page, and the electron is negative, so the force on it is up the page and constant. A constant force perpendicular to the initial velocity gives a parabolic path, up the page (C).
options: A parabolic path down the page
A circular path down the page
A parabolic path up the page
A circular path up the page

questions.question: Which graph could show the relationship between the force between parallel current-carrying conductors and the distance between them?
questions.answer: $\frac Fl=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}$, so $F\propto\frac1d$: a decreasing hyperbola (D).

questions.question: A proton with a velocity of $1.2\times10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ is fired into a uniform magnetic field of $3.0\times10^{-2}$ T, directed out of the page, as shown. It moves in a vacuum in a semi-circle of radius $r$. Which choice best gives the speed of the proton as it exits the magnetic field?
questions.answer: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed is unchanged: $1.2\times10^3\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (B).

questions.question: The arrows in the diagrams represent the motion direction of the magnet or the coil. The speeds are identical in each diagram. Which alternative shows the correct direction of the induced current $I$ in the coil?
questions.answer: By Lenz's law the induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux through the coil caused by the relative motion of the magnet and coil. The direction of $I$ is found by working out whether the flux is increasing or decreasing and applying the right-hand grip rule to the coil. Diagram B matches the school's answer (B).

questions.question: Which wave behaviour provided evidence for the transverse nature of light waves?
questions.answer: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so polarisation showed that light waves are transverse (A).

questions.question: Which is the best description of an electromagnetic wave?
questions.answer: An electromagnetic wave consists of electric and magnetic fields oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (A).
options: Perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields
Perpendicular constant electric and magnetic fields
Radiating parallel electric and magnetic fields

questions.question: A student set up a model generator and attached a galvanometer across the points $X$ and $Y$ (split-ring commutator). Which graph best shows how the current through the meter changes as the coil is rotated $360^\circ$ from the position shown?
questions.answer: A split-ring commutator reverses the connections every half-turn, so the output current always has the same direction, giving a rectified pattern of positive humps that fall to zero twice per rotation. The school's answer is C.

questions.question: A laser beam goes through two close slits $0.10$ mm apart onto a screen $1.6$ m away from the slits. The distance between maximum at $R$ and minimum at $T$ on the interference pattern is $18$ mm. According to the information in the diagram, what is the wavelength of the incident light used in this experiment?
questions.answer: From the diagram, $R$ (a maximum) and $T$ (a minimum) are $2.5$ fringe spacings apart, so $\Delta x=\frac{18}{2.5}=7.2$ mm. $\lambda=\frac{d\,\Delta x}{L}=\frac{0.10\times10^{-3}\times7.2\times10^{-3}}{1.6}=4.5\times10^{-7}$ m (C).

questions.question: Which statement about the spectra of incandescent and laser lights is correct?
questions.answer: An incandescent (black-body) source emits a continuous spectrum over a wide range, while a laser is essentially monochromatic, with a very narrow range of frequencies (A).
options: Incandescent light has a continuous spectrum, laser light has a spectrum specific to its narrow frequency range.
Laser light has a continuous spectrum, incandescent light has a spectrum concentrated in the yellow region.
Laser light has a very wide spectrum concentrated in the infra-red, incandescent has a very narrow spectrum.
Both laser light and incandescent light have a very narrow spectrum.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most accurate statement regarding limitations of special relativity?
questions.answer: Special relativity applies only to inertial (non-accelerating) frames; accelerating frames and gravity require general relativity (D). It has been tested extensively, applies everywhere, and its effects are measurable (if tiny) at low speeds.
options: It has never been tested due to shortcomings in technology
Its equations only apply to space travel
Its effects can only be measured when objects are travelling close to the speed of light
It only applies to inertial frames of reference

questions.question: A rocket is heading directly towards the surface of the Earth at a constant speed of $0.75c$. Physicists on Earth calculate the time that the rocket will take to reach the surface of Earth as $850$ microseconds. How long does the pilot in the rocket calculate it will take him to reach the surface of Earth?
questions.answer: The Earth observers' time is the dilated time $t$; the pilot measures the proper time $t_0=t\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}=850\sqrt{1-0.75^2}=850\times0.6614=562\ \mu$s (A).

questions.question: A road has a curve of radius $63$ m and is banked at an angle of $12^\circ$. The diagram shows a car approaching the curve in wet, slippery conditions. Assuming that there is no friction, calculate the maximum speed at which the car can safely make the turn.
questions.answer: With no friction, $\tan\theta=\frac{v^2}{rg}$, so $v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}=\sqrt{63\times9.8\times\tan12^\circ}=11.45\ \text{m s}^{-1}=41.2\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ (D).

questions.question: A Physics teacher drew two magnetic fields and asked students to explain the difference between the magnetic flux of each field. The two magnetic fields are shown in the diagram. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: Both regions show the same number of field lines (9), so the same flux $\Phi$. The smaller region has the same flux through a smaller area, so a greater flux density $B=\frac\Phi A$ (D).
options: The two magnetic fields show the same amount of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows less flux density.
The two magnetic fields show different amounts of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows less flux density.
The two magnetic fields show different amounts of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows greater flux density.
The two magnetic fields show the same amount of flux, and the smaller magnetic field shows greater flux density.

questions.question: A light meter measures $150\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ of unpolarised light at a fixed position from a light source. A polarising sheet, $P_1$, is placed at this position with an axis of polarisation $30^\circ$ to the vertical. A second polarising sheet, $P_2$, is placed so that any light that passes through $P_1$ also passes through $P_2$. $P_2$ has an axis of polarisation oriented horizontally. What intensity of light is transmitted through $P_2$?
questions.answer: $P_1$ halves unpolarised light: $I_1=75\ \text{W m}^{-2}$. The angle between $P_1$ ($30^\circ$ to vertical) and $P_2$ (horizontal) is $60^\circ$. Malus's law: $I_2=75\cos^260^\circ=18.75\ \text{W m}^{-2}$ (B).

questions.question: The diagram shows a set-up that uses three rods ($A$–$C$), each carrying a current in the direction indicated by the arrows. What is the magnitude and direction of the force per unit length on rod $C$?
questions.answer: Rod $B$ (4 A, 20 cm away) has current in the same direction as $C$, so attracts it (up): $\frac Fl=\frac{\mu_0 I_BI_C}{2\pi d}=2\times10^{-7}\frac{4\times5}{0.20}=2\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ up. Rod $A$ (3 A, 30 cm away) has current opposite to $C$, so repels it (down): $2\times10^{-7}\frac{3\times5}{0.30}=1\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$ down. Net $=1\times10^{-5}\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ up (B).

questions.question: A conducting rod is rolling horizontally along a metal conducting loop in a magnetic field (into the page), as shown in the diagram. Which row of the table is correct?
questions.answer: The loop's area (flux into the page) is increasing as the rod moves right, so the induced current creates a field out of the page: anticlockwise. By Lenz's law the magnetic force on the rod opposes its motion (to the left), so the rod slows, the emf $\varepsilon=Blv$ falls and the globe dims (A).
options: Force on the rod: to the left; current around the loop: anticlockwise; brightness of the light globe: decreasing
Force on the rod: to the left; current around the loop: clockwise; brightness of the light globe: constant
Force on the rod: to the right; current around the loop: anticlockwise; brightness of the light globe: decreasing
Force on the rod: to the right; current around the loop: clockwise; brightness of the light globe: constant

questions.question: The diagram shows a totem tennis set-up, as viewed from above. A tennis ball is tied to a pole with a cord so that it moves in a clockwise, circular motion around the centre pole. Label the velocity of the ball and the forces acting on it at the point shown in the diagram. Explain your answer.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The ball's velocity is tangent to the circle, in the direction of motion (down the page at the point shown, since the motion is clockwise). The tension in the cord acts towards the centre of the circle, and the weight force acts vertically downwards (into the page when viewed from above). The ball is accelerating towards the centre of the circle, so the net force is the centripetal force, which here is provided by the horizontal component of the tension. Gravity acts downwards, and the vertical component of the tension balances it. The velocity is a tangent to the circle in the direction of the motion of the ball.

questions.question: The ball has a mass of 60.0 g and the cord is 1.80 m long. The ball rotates around the centre pole at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the pole. Calculate the radius of the ball's circular path.
questions.answer: $\sin45^\circ=\frac r{1.80}$, so $r=1.80\sin45^\circ=1.27$ m.

questions.question: The ball has a mass of 60.0 g and rotates around the centre pole at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the pole. Determine the magnitude of the net force acting on the ball at the point shown.
questions.answer: The vertical component of the tension balances the weight: $F_T\cos45^\circ=mg=0.0600\times9.8=0.588$ N. The net (centripetal) force is the horizontal component, $F_{net}=F_T\sin45^\circ=mg\tan45^\circ=0.588$ N $\approx0.59$ N, directed towards the centre. (The school's diagram labels the weight as 1.96 N, which does not match $0.0600$ kg, but its working and answer of $0.59$ N are correct.)

questions.question: In an experiment involving an evacuated gas tube, electrons were accelerated from rest through a voltage of 2400 V, then entered a uniform magnetic field strength of $1.8\times10^{-3}$ T at right angles to the electron beam. Calculate the speed of these electrons upon entering the magnetic field.
questions.answer: The work done by the electric field becomes kinetic energy: $qV=\frac12mv^2$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2qV}{m}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\times1.6\times10^{-19}\times2400}{9.1\times10^{-31}}}=2.9\times10^{7}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (The magnetic field does not change the speed.)

questions.question: In science, observations lead to hypotheses and further experimentation. Robert Millikan conducted experiments to determine the charge on an electron. One of these experiments is shown in the diagram (plates $2.5$ cm apart connected to a $4500$ V supply, with a charged oil drop between them). Explain the observations Millikan made that led to his determination of the charge of an electron.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Millikan observed oil drops falling through the small gap between the plates. When the electric force was equal to the opposing gravitational force, the drop remained in static equilibrium, so $mg=qE$ where $E=\frac Vd$ (here $E=\frac{4500}{0.025}=1.8\times10^5\ \text{V m}^{-1}$). From this he calculated the charge on each drop. He observed that the charge on the oil droplets was always a whole-number multiple of $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, which is the charge on an electron.

questions.question: The diagram shows a strobe photo of a ball projected into the air. The camera took 7 images per second of the ball. What was the maximum height of the ball above the ground?
questions.answer: From the highest point there are 6 image intervals to the ground, so the fall time is $t=\frac67$ s, with vertical velocity zero at the top. $s=ut+\frac12at^2=0+4.9\left(\frac67\right)^2=3.6$ m. The maximum height is $3.6$ m.

questions.question: The table shows data for three of the moons of Jupiter. On the axes provided, graph relevant data to verify Kepler's Law of Periods. Include a line of best fit.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Plot $r^3$ (vertical axis, $\times10^{26}\ \text{m}^3$) against $T^2$ (horizontal axis, $\times10^{10}\ \text{s}^2$): points $(2.34,1.2)$, $(9.61,4.1)$, $(38.4,14.9)$ with a ruled straight line of best fit through them, passing through the origin, with labelled axes and units.

questions.question: The graph of $r^3$ against $T^2$ for the three moons of Jupiter is a straight line through the origin. Explain how the graph provides evidence for Kepler's law of periods.
questions.answer: Sample answer: From Kepler's law, $\frac{r^3}{T^2}=\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}=$ constant, which is the gradient of the graph. Since the graph has a constant gradient (a straight line through the origin), it shows that Kepler's law of periods holds for these three moons of Jupiter.

questions.question: Using the graph of $r^3$ against $T^2$ (gradient about $\dfrac{8\times10^{26}}{20\times10^{10}}=4\times10^{15}\ \text{m}^3\text{s}^{-2}$), determine the mass of Jupiter.
questions.answer: The gradient is $\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}$, so $M=\frac{4\pi^2}{G}\times\text{gradient}=\frac{4\pi^2\times4\times10^{15}}{6.67\times10^{-11}}=2.4\times10^{27}$ kg.

questions.question: The diagram below shows a simple electric motor. The square coil $WXYZ$ has sides of 4.0 cm and lies completely in the horizontal uniform magnetic field $B$ of strength 2.0 T. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the sides $WZ$ and $XY$. The coil has 20 turns and rotates about the axis shown. The current drawn from the battery is 2.5 A. For the position of the coil in the diagram, determine the torque on the side $WZ$.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Force on $WZ$: $F=nBIl=20\times2.0\times2.5\times0.040=4.0$ N. By the right-hand push rule the force on $WZ$ is upwards. The distance from the axis is half the coil width, $2.0\times10^{-2}$ m, so $\tau=Fd=4.0\times2.0\times10^{-2}=8.0\times10^{-2}$ N m, directed to rotate the coil upwards on the $WZ$ side.

questions.question: Explain the continuous movement of the coil in a simple DC motor in relation to the changing torque acting on the coil.
questions.answer: Sample answer: As the coil rotates, the torque on sides $WZ$ and $XY$ reduces to zero, as the perpendicular distance from the force to the axis of rotation reduces to zero. The momentum of the coil moves it past the vertical position. In the vertical position, the commutator setup changes the direction of the current in the coil and hence the direction of the torque acting on $WZ$ and $XY$ is changed every $180^\circ$, resulting in continuous rotation.

questions.question: Using a mass spectrometer, some students did an experiment to determine the relationship between the charge on a particle and its radius of curvature in a magnetic field. The diagram shows the path of only two of the six charged particles observed. Their results: charge (electronic charges) 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 gave radii of curvature ($\times10^{-11}$ m) of 6.1, 2.9, 2.1, 1.5, 1.2, 0.9. The students plotted their results (radius against number of charges, a smooth falling curve) and concluded that the radius of curvature of a charge in a magnetic field is inversely proportional to the magnitude of the charge. Evaluate their conclusion and identify any problems with their method.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The conclusion is invalid. A conclusion cannot be made because the graph is not a straight line, so their conclusion cannot be based on a graph plotting radius against charge (they would need to plot $r$ against $\frac1q$ to test for inverse proportionality). Also, the experiment description does not have the necessary controlled variables stated: the mass and velocity of the charged particles will affect the radius of curvature, as well as the charge. Centripetal force: $\frac{mv^2}{r}=Bqv$, so $r=\frac{mv}{B}\times\frac1q$. This shows that radius is inversely proportional to charge only if mass and velocity are constant, as well as the magnetic field.

questions.question: The rest life, or proper lifetime, of a meson is $2.5\times10^{-8}$ s. An observer measures the distance travelled by a meson moving at $2.95\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in the laboratory. Compare the expected distance travelled by the meson in the absence of time dilation with the distance that would be measured by the observer.
questions.answer: Time in the observer's frame: $t=\frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}=\frac{2.5\times10^{-8}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2.95\times10^8}{3.0\times10^8}\right)^2}}=1.37\times10^{-7}$ s. The observer measures $s=vt=2.95\times10^8\times1.37\times10^{-7}=40.4$ m (with time dilation). Without time dilation, $s=vt=2.95\times10^8\times2.5\times10^{-8}=7.38$ m. So the observer measures about $5.5$ times the distance expected without time dilation.

questions.question: A spacecraft of mass 79 000 kg is moving at $0.3c$. Compare the momentum of the spacecraft measured by the spacecraft's pilot with the momentum measured by an external observer, and explain why objects cannot accelerate to the speed of light.
questions.answer: The pilot is inside the spacecraft, so would assume their momentum to be 0 kg m s$^{-1}$. For the external observer, $p_v=\frac{m_0v}{\sqrt{1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}}}=\frac{79000\times0.3\times3.0\times10^8}{\sqrt{1-0.3^2}}=7.45\times10^{12}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ (about $7\times10^{12}$). As the speed approaches $c$, the momentum (or relativistic mass) approaches infinity, so an infinite amount of energy would be needed to reach the speed of light, so an object with mass cannot accelerate to the speed of light.

questions.question: The diagram represents an important experiment done by a group of scientists in 1907 (alpha particles from a radium source striking gold foil, with a fluorescent screen around it). Outline the background to the experiment, its results and the proposed model of the atom based on the experimental results.
questions.answer: Sample answer: This experiment, eventually known as the Rutherford alpha particle scattering experiment, was done by two of Rutherford's postgraduate students, Geiger and Marsden. It had been shown that alpha particles were deflected when passing through very thin gold foil, and it was not understood how this occurred based on Thomson's plum pudding model of the atom, a random arrangement of positive and negative charge. Rutherford expected that the alpha particles would pass through the gold foil with very small deflections. Most of the alpha particles were observed to pass straight through the foil or to be scattered only one or two degrees. The surprising result was that a few alpha particles were observed to be scattered at larger angles and a very few were reflected almost straight back. Rutherford proposed that the force causing the large deflections and repulsion of the positively charged alpha particles could only be caused by a positively charged small object with concentrated mass in the centre of the gold atoms. He also proposed that this centre, called the nucleus, was surrounded by a much larger region of mainly empty space and circling electrons, too small to cause the occasional deflections of the alpha particles. Rutherford's new model of the atom was able to explain the experimental results of the alpha particle scattering experiments.

questions.question: A student sets up an aluminium disc which is able to rotate in the vertical plane. The axle of the disc has a pulley wheel turned by a motor in series with an ammeter, battery and switch. A clamp with a horseshoe magnet can be attached so that a horizontal magnetic field passes through one part of the disc. The student observes the current and the speed of disc rotation, before and after the magnet is attached with its magnetic field passing through the disc. When the magnet is in place, the current through the ammeter is more and the speed of rotation of the disc is less. By applying Lenz's Law, explain each observation.
questions.answer: Sample answer: When a motor is switched on, the motion of the motor's rotating coil in its magnetic field will induce a back emf in the coil according to Faraday's law of induction. The direction of this emf must be such that it opposes the motion of the coil (Lenz's law) and therefore does not contravene the law of conservation of energy. The net voltage decreases, and therefore the current through the motor is less. The back emf is proportional to the rotational speed of the motor coil.\n\nWhen the horseshoe magnet surrounds part of the aluminium disc, eddy currents are set up in the disc because the disc is a conductor moving in a magnetic field (changing flux). By Lenz's law, the direction of the currents will be such as to oppose the magnetic field and oppose the motion of the disc, which is known as the braking effect, reducing the rotational speed of the disc and the motor coil. Consequently the back emf is also less, so the net emf (supply emf minus back emf) is greater, resulting in the greater current seen on the ammeter.

questions.question: For electricity to be transmitted over the large distances between generators and households, transformers are used. Two transmissions take place over the same transmission lines. In transmission A, energy is transmitted at 28 kV AC. In transmission B, the same amount of energy is transmitted at 280 kV AC. Compare the power losses that occur in transmissions A and B. Include relevant equations and calculations in your response.
questions.answer: Sample answer: $P=VI$ so for the same power the current is inversely proportional to the voltage. The voltage in B is 10 times greater than in A, so the current in A must be ten times that in B. $P_{loss}=I^2R$: with the same line resistance $R$, $P_{loss,B}=\left(\frac1{10}\right)^2P_{loss,A}$, so transmission B loses $\frac1{100}$ of the power lost in A (A loses 100 times more). Less energy is wasted as heat in the lines at the higher voltage, in line with conservation of energy.

questions.question: In the 1840s, French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau performed an experiment to measure the speed of light. He shone an intense light source at a mirror 8 km away and broke up the light beam with a rotating cogwheel. He adjusted the speed of rotation of the wheel until the reflected light beam could no longer be seen returning through the gaps in the cogwheel. The diagram shows a similar experiment. The cogwheel has 50 teeth and 50 gaps of the same width. Explain why specific speeds of rotation of the cogwheel will completely block the returning light. Support your answer with calculations.
questions.answer: Sample answer: Light travels at $3.00\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, so for an 8 km journey to the mirror and 8 km back the time taken is $t=\frac{2\times8000}{3.00\times10^8}=5.33\times10^{-5}$ s. If the wheel is stationary, light travelling through a gap will return completely through the gap, but if the wheel is rotating, a tooth will begin to block the returning light. If a tooth moves exactly the width of a gap in the time it takes the light to return, it will completely block the light. To completely block the light, the tooth must move into the path of a gap in this time. Since there are 50 teeth and 50 gaps, the wheel will have rotated $\frac1{100}$th of a rotation, which is $\frac{2\pi}{100}$ radians. The rotational speed is $\omega=\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}=\frac{2\pi/100}{5.33\times10^{-5}}=1180\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$. Spinning the cogwheel at 3, 5 and 7 times this rate (any odd multiple) would also completely block the returning light, as the light will be blocked by subsequent teeth.

questions.question: A communications company launched a satellite of mass 250 kg. The satellite is in an orbit with an altitude of 27 129 km above the Earth. Calculate the gravitational potential energy of the satellite and its escape velocity. In your response, explain what the term 'escape velocity' means.
questions.answer: The orbital radius is $r=27\,129\text{ km}+6371\text{ km}\approx3.35\times10^7$ m. $U=-\frac{GMm}{r}=-\frac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times6.0\times10^{24}\times250}{3.35\times10^7}=-2.99\times10^9$ J. The escape velocity is the minimum speed that the satellite requires to escape Earth's gravitational field; this occurs when the satellite's kinetic energy is equal to the magnitude of the gravitational potential energy: $\frac12mv^2=|U|$, so $v=\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r}}=4888\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (about $4.9$ km s$^{-1}$).

questions.question: In an experiment, students used a light source that emitted a wide range of frequencies. They used filters so that only specific frequencies could fall onto a photoelectric plate. Most of the filters produced frequencies which did not cause emission. Julie says that if the intensities of these frequencies were increased, emission will occur. They experimented with this variable and found that emission still did not occur. Explain the student's observations and how they provide evidence for the nature of light.
questions.answer:
Sample answer: This result can only be explained if light waves are made up of particles, packets of wave energy called photons. The term 'intensity', when applied to electromagnetic radiations, refers to the number of photons in a beam; it does not refer to an increase in the energy of each photon. That is, increasing intensity means more photons, but each has the same energy.

For the photoelectric emission of electrons, the electrons must receive an amount of energy known as the work function of the material, to enable the electron to be emitted. One photon has to have greater energy than the work function for emission to occur ($K_{max}=hf-\phi$, with $E=hf$), so below the threshold frequency no emission occurs, which would explain why increasing the intensity did not result in emission, as Julie predicted.

If the light photons were waves, then the electrons of the emitter would be subjected to a continuous supply of energy and eventually, if the intensity is increased, enough would be absorbed to cause emission at any frequency. The fact that this does not happen means that these observations provide evidence for the particle nature of light. Experiments show that light does exhibit wave behaviour and is described as having a dual nature.

questions.question: In science, there is a close link between developments in technology and developments in knowledge and understanding. Evaluate this statement with reference to the cathode ray debate and Thomson's discovery of the electron.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The statement is well supported. Developments in technology enabled new observations that changed understanding of the nature of cathode rays. High voltage supplies (e.g. induction coils) connected to cathode and anode in evacuated Crookes tubes (vacuum technology) produced cathode rays. Modified tubes, such as the Maltese cross and paddle-wheel tubes, showed that the rays travel in straight lines and carry momentum (supporting the particle view), while a thin gold foil or fluorescent screen allowed the rays to be observed. Electromagnets and oppositely charged electric plates were used to deflect the beam, and Thomson's experiment, using both fields to balance the deflections, determined the charge-to-mass ratio $\\frac{q}{m}$ of the particles, showing that they were negatively charged and much smaller than atoms, so a new subatomic particle, the electron, had been discovered. Each technological advance (better vacuum pumps, fluorescent screens, field plates and electromagnets) therefore supplied the evidence that resolved the debate between the wave (aether) and particle models of cathode rays and led to the development of knowledge about atomic structure.
